name: Tara Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Tara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Millbrook Garden and Hardware Wholesale. Spades, hose reels, compost, paint, screws, that sort of thing for garden centres and hardware shops across the county. I ring the suppliers, check the order book, and walk the warehouse with the stock sheet because I don't trust the screen on its own. Dennis Marsh owns the place and Sue, who's sixty and been buying for thirty years, still signs off anything big. I'm three years in and still the new one.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Ken supervises road maintenance crews for the council, so he's steady, and we've got Lottie, twelve, and Finn, nine. We've a mortgage on a three-bed in Fairfield, and we've been careful, I'd say about eight months of savings. I do the packed lunches, Ken does the football runs, and we both mind the pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's no surprise, there's always a new miracle and it's usually a lot of fuss. At work I'd say nothing, I'd just keep doing what works. To friends I'd say wait till you see it do something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'm not totally easy, though not because of AI. Millbrook is small and the big warehouses keep undercutting Dennis. If a bit of software shaves a clerk's hours I'd bet it's one of ours that gets the push, and I'm the newest buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, and keep my stock sheet and my phone book of suppliers. I'd ask Sue to teach me more about the big accounts, since she's near retiring. We'd carry on putting 250 a month away and wouldn't touch the holiday fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit watchful. Not frightened, just aware. Spring is our big season and a bad spring is more worrying than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Millbrook has to watch costs. Does that matter in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a tool turned up I'd try it for a week and see if it helped. If it got something wrong I'd say so plainly and go back to the old way. I'm slow with new things, I'll admit, because I'd rather be right than quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do if a tool turns up and you're told to try it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money first. If Dennis lost a big customer, he'd cut people before he cut his own pay. And I'd feel that more than any robot.

say: I'd say there's always a new miracle and it's usually a lot of **fuss**.
At work I'd say nothing and keep doing what **works**.
think: I'm not totally easy, because Millbrook is small and the big warehouses keep **undercutting** Dennis.
As the newest buyer I'd be the first one **cut** if software shaves a clerk's hours.
do: Keep my stock **sheet** and my phone book of suppliers.
Ask Sue to teach me more about the big **accounts** before she retires.
Keep putting **250** a month away and leave the holiday fund alone.
feel: **Watchful**, not frightened, because a bad spring worries me more than any computer.
S0.quote: A bad spring is more worrying than any computer.
fieldNote: Her worry is the small firm's margins, not AI itself.
Resists tools by habit: she would rather be right than quick.
Newest buyer, so she feels any trimming **first**.

steps.text: Keep the paper stock sheet and supplier phone book going
Ask Sue to teach her the big account relationships
Put away 250 a month and leave the holiday fund alone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening whether we like it or not, and that I'd rather it came with some rules. At work I'd keep my head down and watch which tasks get moved to the software first. To friends I'd say I'm not thrilled, but I'm not going to shout about it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frankly I think the buying desk is exactly where this lands. Checking stock, comparing quotes, reordering, that's most of my week. I'm the junior and I don't use any of these tools, so I'd be the obvious one to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by getting the facts: ask Dennis straight what the plan is for the buying team. I'd put a little more away each month, maybe 400, and tell Ken we'd go easy on extras. I'd also ask my cousin who works at a bank whether there'd be admin work there, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the stomach. I'm not panicking, but I'm not sleeping like a baby either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Ken about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, look, they're going to change how my job works, and I might be one of the ones who has to find something else. I'd tell him that we'd be fine for a while, because we have the savings and he has a steady job. I'd just want us both to be honest about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Millbrook would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sue because she's sixty and might be pushed to retire early, and the two girls in the order office, who do the type of task a computer is good at. I'd worry about the warehouse lads less, because they lift things and software can't.

say: I'd say it's happening whether we like it or not, and I'd rather it came with some **rules**.
At work I'd keep my head down and watch which tasks go to software **first**.
think: The buying desk is exactly where this lands, since checking stock and comparing quotes is most of my **week**.
As a junior who uses none of these tools, I'd be the **obvious** one to go.
do: Ask Dennis straight what the **plan** is for the buying team.
Put away **400** a month and go easy on extras.
Ask my cousin at the bank whether there'd be **admin** work there.
feel: **Tight** in the stomach, not panicking but not sleeping like a baby.
S1.quote: I might be one of the ones who has to find something else.
fieldNote: Recognises her own tasks in the card and is blunt that she's the obvious cut.
Avoids new tools but still acts: asks the boss directly and starts a backup plan.
Savings and **Ken's** council job keep her from alarm.

steps.text: Ask Dennis directly what the plan is for the buying team
Save 400 a month and go easy on extras
Ask her cousin about admin work at the bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster waiting to happen if nobody's ready. At work I'd say let's slow down and make sure people aren't dropped. I'd probably tell friends that the council and the government need to get on top of it or we'll all be on the same queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is finished, I think. Two years and the computer does the whole buying side, maybe within one year of the company getting it. Robots for the warehouse come three years later, so the lads have a bit longer, but I don't have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd freeze everything we don't need: new bathroom, trips, the lot. I'd put the lot into savings, and I'd talk to the bank early about what they could do on the mortgage. I'd also ask Ken whether the council has any admin roles, because public work is slower to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly worried. It's a two-year clock and I'm not good at jumping fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is quick. What's the first thing that goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd guess the first thing to go wrong is Dennis telling me they don't need as many buyers, then telling Sue she can go early, then the girls in the order office. All the same month. It'd be quick and nobody will have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Ken's job at the council was fine, how long could you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On savings alone with Ken's wage we could hold on for perhaps a year and a half if we were careful. But I wouldn't want to touch the cushion, because I'd have to find something new and that costs money to retrain for. I'd rather get a job quick than a perfect one.

say: I'd say it's a **disaster** waiting to happen if nobody's ready, and we should slow down so people aren't dropped.
I'd tell friends the **government** needs to get on top of it.
think: My buying job is **finished**, because the computer does the whole buying side within about two years.
Robots reach the warehouse three years later, so the lads get **longer** than I do.
do: Freeze everything **extra**: the bathroom, the trips, the lot.
Talk to the bank early about what they could do on the **mortgage**.
Ask Ken whether the **council** has any admin roles.
feel: Properly **worried**, because it's a two-year clock and I'm not good at jumping fast.
S2.quote: My job is finished, I think.
fieldNote: Believes her desk work is finished on the stated date but the warehouse team gets about three more years.
Wants a **quick** job, not a perfect one, which shows her dislike of risk.
Plans around her husband's slower public-sector job.

steps.text: Freeze the bathroom, trips and other extras
Talk to the bank early about mortgage options
Ask Ken about admin roles at the council
Put all spare money into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit of breathing space, but not a lot. At work I'd say we should start thinking about it now, even if I'd rather not. I'd tell friends that governments ought to set up training, but I wouldn't hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two. I still think my buying job goes, but I'd have time to look for something else and not be in a rush. I'm not the sort to jump early though, I'd wait until I could see which jobs are actually going to last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Millbrook while it lasts and put more into savings, maybe 450 a month. I'd go on a short course at the college in something that isn't buying, probably payroll or stock control. I'd also ask Sue if I could take on the customer visits, since people stay in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit calmer than the first, but still anxious. It's something sitting in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you do anything different from the two-year case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm offer from somewhere solid. Not a promise of a shiny job, but a council or a hospital, somewhere that will still be there. I'd rather have steady than exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tempt you to change job early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot. I'd just start the course and the extra saving sooner. In two years I'd be scrambling, in five I'd at least be walking.

say: I'd say five years is a bit of breathing space, but not a **lot**, so we should start thinking now.
I'd tell friends governments ought to set up **training**.
think: Five years is better than two, but my buying job still goes and I'd rather not **jump** early.
I'd wait until I can see which jobs will actually **last**.
do: Take a short college course in payroll or **stock** control.
Ask Sue if I can take on the customer **visits**.
feel: A bit **calmer** than the first, but still anxious, with it sitting at the back of my head.
S3.quote: In two years I'd be scrambling, in five I'd at least be walking.
fieldNote: Prefers a steady employer over an exciting one, consistent with her risk-averse profile.
Only acts early on small, safe things like a **course** and extra saving.
Won't jump until she sees which jobs last.

steps.text: Take a college course in payroll or stock control
Ask Sue to let her take over customer visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good while, so everyone's got time to get ready if they're sensible. At work I'd say no rush, but let's keep an eye on it. To friends I'd say it'll be fine if people look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be fifty-three, Lottie would be at university, Finn nearly done with school. I think my buying job does go by then, but it's a long way off and I don't think I'd feel it as a shock. I'd have time to settle into something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and save for the kids' university fees. I'd probably do a part-time course in something like stock control or office management when the kids are older. And I'd keep an eye on how the firm is getting on, since small firms either adapt or close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit of worry about Dennis keeping Millbrook going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a long time. If Dennis's firm is still going in five years I'll be surprised, to be honest. The big ones swallow the small ones, with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lottie and Finn about jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get a trade or a skill you can use with your hands and your head, and don't count on a desk. Be the person who can turn up and fix a problem. Ken's job is a good example, there's always a road to mend.

say: I'd say ten years is a good while, so there's **time** to get ready if people are sensible.
To friends I'd say it'll be fine if people look after each **other**.
think: My buying job goes by then, but it's far off and I wouldn't feel it as a **shock**.
If Dennis's firm is still going in five years I'll be **surprised**, with or without AI.
do: Carry on as I am and save for the kids' **university** fees.
Do a part-time **course** in stock control or office management once the kids are older.
Keep an eye on how **Millbrook** is getting on.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a bit of worry about Dennis keeping the firm going.
S4.quote: Get a trade or a skill you can use with your hands and your head, and don't count on a desk.
fieldNote: Long time horizon lowers panic but she stays anxious because of the firm's fragility.
Her advice to her children is rooted in her husband's **road work**.
Still resistant: she plans to wait and see rather than move early.

steps.text: Save for Lottie's and Finn's university fees
Study stock control part-time when the kids are older
Watch how Millbrook is doing and wait to decide

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time and I'm not a quick mover. What'd help is some notice from Dennis, a course I can do while still being paid, and a council or hospital job that's stable. And Ken staying in his job, which I touch wood about.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not stupid, I'm just slow with new things. I'd rather be careful than caught out. I'd say most people are the same, they just won't tell you.

headlineQuote: I'm not stupid, I'm just slow with new things. I'd rather be careful than caught out.
portrait: Tara is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at Millbrook Garden and Hardware Wholesale, three years in and still learning.
She never uses AI, trusts her paper stock sheet and her phone book of **suppliers**, and likes steady over exciting.
Her husband Ken works for the council, they have two children, a mortgage and about eight months of savings.
She reads the card closely and expects her **desk** job to go, but acts early only on small, safe moves.
Her real worry is a small firm being **undercut** by the big warehouses, with or without AI.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because she's slow to change and has no time.
whatWouldHelp: Early **notice** from her boss, paid retraining time, and a steady council or hospital job.
